paragraphs: It struck me long ago that the advice on conduct, and all the many ways of keeping a good reputation, which have been pressed so insistently upon women, were poisons in attractive disguise, which put a crust over morality while they ate away its substance. It struck me, too, that this measuring of shadows yielded a false reckoning, since their length depends so much on the height of the sun and on other chance circumstances.

What is the source of a courtier’s smooth, deceitful manner? Without doubt, his situation: because he needs people to depend on him, he must learn the art of refusing without causing offence, and of evasively nourishing hope on the chameleon’s food of air. In this way politeness makes a game of truth, and, by eating away the sincerity and humanity natural to man, turns out the fine gentleman.

In the same way, women acquire, out of a supposed necessity, an equally artificial manner of behaving. Yet no one can trifle with truth and go unpunished, for the practised deceiver ends by being taken in by his own tricks, and loses the shrewdness that has rightly been called common sense — that is, a quick grasp of common truths, which the unsophisticated mind always accepts as truths, even though it might not have had the energy to discover them for itself when local prejudices obscured them. Most people take their opinions on trust to spare themselves the trouble of using their own minds, and such lazy beings naturally cling to the letter rather than the spirit of a law, whether divine or human. “Women,” says some author whose name I cannot remember, “mind not what only heaven sees.” And why, indeed, should they? It is the eye of man that they have been taught to fear — and if they can lull their Argus to sleep, they seldom give a thought to heaven or to themselves, because their reputation is safe; and it is reputation, not chastity and all its fair train, that they are busy keeping free of stains, not as a virtue but in order to hold on to their place in the world.

To prove this remark true, I need only point to the love affairs of married women, especially in high society, and in countries where parents marry their daughters off suitably, according to their rank. If an innocent girl falls a victim to love, she is disgraced for ever, although her mind has not been corrupted by the arts that married women practise under the convenient cover of marriage; nor has she broken any duty except the duty of respecting herself. The married woman, by contrast, breaks a most sacred commitment, and turns into a cruel mother when she becomes a false and faithless wife. If her husband still loves her, the tricks she has to use to deceive him will make her the most contemptible of human beings; and in any case the schemes needed to keep up appearances will hold her mind in that childish or vicious agitation which destroys all its energy. Moreover, in time, like people who habitually take cordials to lift their spirits, she will need an intrigue to put life into her thoughts, having lost all taste for pleasures that are not strongly spiced with hope or fear.
Married women sometimes behave even more brazenly; I will give one example.

A woman of rank, notorious for her love affairs — though, since she still lived with her husband, nobody chose to put her in the class where she belonged — made a point of treating with the most insulting contempt a poor timid creature, still ashamed of her earlier weakness, whom a gentleman of the neighbourhood had seduced and later married. This woman had actually mistaken reputation for virtue; and I truly believe she prided herself on how properly she had behaved before her marriage, although once she was settled to her family’s satisfaction, she and her lord were as unfaithful as each other — so that the half-alive heir to a vast estate came from heaven knows where!
Let me look at this subject from another side.

I have known many women who, if they did not love their husbands, loved no one else, yet gave themselves over wholly to vanity and dissipation and neglected every household duty — indeed, even wasted all the money that ought to have been put aside for their helpless younger children — and who still preened themselves on their spotless reputation, as though the entire scope of their duty as wives and mothers were simply to keep it intact. Other idle women, meanwhile, neglecting every duty they personally owed, have supposed that they earned their husbands’ affection because they behaved properly in this one respect.

Weak minds always like to rest in the ceremonies of duty, but morality offers far simpler motives; and one could wish that shallow moralists had said less about behaviour and outward observances, for unless virtue of any kind is founded on knowledge, it will produce nothing but a sort of insipid decency. Nevertheless, respect for the world’s opinion has been called, in the plainest terms, woman’s chief duty, for Rousseau declares, “that reputation is no less indispensable than chastity.” “A man,” he adds, “secure in his own good conduct, depends only on himself, and may brave the public opinion; but a woman, in behaving well, performs but half her duty; as what is thought of her, is as important to her as what she really is. It follows hence, that the system of a woman’s education should, in this respect, be directly contrary to that of ours. Opinion is the grave of virtue among the men; but its throne among women.” It is strictly logical to conclude that a virtue resting on opinion is purely worldly, and that it is the virtue of a being who has been denied reason. But even as regards the world’s opinion, I am convinced that reasoners of this kind are wrong.

This concern for reputation, however — quite apart from its being one of the natural rewards of virtue — arose from a cause I have already lamented as the chief source of female depravity: the impossibility of recovering respectability by returning to virtue, although men keep theirs while they indulge in vice. It was natural, then, for women to try to hold on to what, once lost, was lost for ever, until this concern swallowed up every other, and a reputation for chastity became the one thing needful to the sex. But the anxious scruples of ignorance are futile, for neither religion nor virtue, when they dwell in the heart, demands such childish attention to mere ceremonies, since conduct must on the whole be right when the motive is pure.

In support of my opinion I can cite very respectable authority; and the authority of a cool reasoner ought to carry enough weight to compel consideration, though not to settle an opinion. Speaking of the general laws of morality, Dr. Smith observes — “That by some very extraordinary and unlucky circumstance, a good man may come to be suspected of a crime of which he was altogether incapable, and upon that account be most unjustly exposed for the remaining part of his life to the horror and aversion of mankind. By an accident of this kind he may be said to lose his all, notwithstanding his integrity and justice, in the same manner as a cautious man, notwithstanding his utmost circumspection, may be ruined by an earthquake or an inundation. Accidents of the first kind, however, are perhaps still more rare, and still more contrary to the common course of things than those of the second; and it still remains true, that the practice of truth, justice and humanity, is a certain and almost infallible method of acquiring what those virtues chiefly aim at, the confidence and love of those we live with. A person may be easily misrepresented with regard to a particular action; but it is scarcely possible that he should be so with regard to the general tenor of his conduct. An innocent man may be believed to have done wrong: this, however, will rarely happen. On the contrary, the established opinion of the innocence of his manners will often lead us to absolve him where he has really been in the fault, notwithstanding very strong presumptions.”

I entirely share this writer’s opinion, for I truly believe that few people of either sex have ever been despised for certain vices without deserving it. I am not speaking of the passing slander that hangs over a character like one of the thick November fogs over this capital, until it slowly lifts before the ordinary light of day; I only maintain that the daily conduct of most people prevails in stamping their character with the mark of truth. Quietly, day after day, the clear light shines and disproves the ignorant guess or the malicious story that has thrown mud on a pure character. For a short time a false light distorted its shadow — reputation; but that shadow seldom fails to become accurate once the cloud that caused the error of vision has dispersed.

Many people, no doubt, in several respects win a better reputation than, strictly speaking, they deserve, for untiring effort will usually reach its goal in every race. Those who strive only for this paltry prize, like the Pharisees who prayed at the street corners to be seen of men, truly obtain the reward they are after; for the heart of man cannot be read by man! Still, the good name that good actions naturally reflect, when a man is concerned only to walk rightly, without regard to the onlookers, is generally not only truer but also more secure.

There are, admittedly, ordeals in which the good man must appeal from the injustice of man to God, and, amid the whining of candour or the hissing of envy, set up a pavilion in his own mind to withdraw into until the rumour has passed; indeed, the darts of undeserved blame may pierce an innocent, tender heart through with many sorrows. But all these are exceptions to general rules, and it is by these common laws that human conduct should be governed. The eccentric orbit of a comet never affects astronomers’ calculations of the unchanging order established in the movement of the main bodies of the solar system.

I will therefore venture to state that, once a man has reached maturity, the general outline of his character as the world sees it is accurate, allowing for the exceptions to the rule mentioned above. I do not claim that a prudent, worldly-wise man, with only negative virtues and qualities, may not sometimes gain a smoother reputation than a wiser or better man. Far from it: experience inclines me to conclude that where two people are almost equal in virtue, the world at large will like the more negative character better, while the other may have more friends in private life. But the hills and valleys, the clouds and sunshine, so visible in the virtues of great men, set one another off; and although they give envious weakness a better target, the real character will still make its way into the light, however much it is spattered by weak affection or clever malice.*
(*Footnote. I am alluding to various biographical writings, but above all to Boswell’s Life of Johnson.)

As for that anxiety to protect a reputation hardly won, which leads shrewd people to analyse it, I will not make the obvious comment; but I fear that morality is being very insidiously undermined among women by turning their attention to the show rather than the substance. In this way a simple thing becomes strangely complicated; indeed, virtue and its shadow are sometimes set against each other. We should perhaps never have heard of Lucretia if she had died to preserve her chastity rather than her reputation. If we truly deserve our own good opinion, the world will usually respect us; but if we long for higher improvement and higher attainments, it is not enough to look at ourselves as we imagine others look at us, although this has been ingeniously put forward as the basis of our moral sentiments. (Smith.) For every bystander may have his own prejudices, in addition to those of his age or country. We should rather try to see ourselves as we imagine that Being sees us who watches each thought ripen into action, and whose judgment never departs from the eternal rule of right. Righteous are all his judgments — just, as merciful!
